q-37623.name: Question 1
q-37623.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $G$ that has eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
q-37623.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $G,$ then $G$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $G=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $G,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
G={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}G & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & 24 \\ 18 & 40\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 12 \\ -30 & 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-86678.name: Question 2
q-86678.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $S$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
q-86678.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $S,$ then $S$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $S=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $S,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
S={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -7 & 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -7 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -7 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}40 & -2 \\ 35 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -7 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}54 & -56 \\ 49 & -51\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-140129.name: Question 3
q-140129.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $C$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
q-140129.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $C,$ then $C$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 12 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

q-140130.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A$, then  $A$ must be diagonalizable. 

So, we can write $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $A$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-81214.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $H$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$
q-81214.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $H,$ then $H$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $H=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $H,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
H={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}H & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 21 \\ 4 & -14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 15 \\ -10 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-86686.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{85} & =P{D}^{85}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{85}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{85} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{85}\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-37597.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{97} & =P{D}^{97}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{97}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(-1)^{97} & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{97}\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
{N}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.

$$

We have been given the following diagonalization of $M.$

$$
M={{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[32]{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $M=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${M}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{M}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}^{32} & =P{D}^{32}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[32]{3}\end{aligned}]}^{32}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{32} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[32]{3})^{32}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ 5 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-29 & 48 \\ -20 & 33\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-40138.name: Question 11
q-40138.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
B[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
q-40138.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$ 

$$
B={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$
$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 11

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix B given that B[3411]=[3411][0002].

a
[01] and [32]
b
[−14] and [1−3]
c
[31] and [41]
d
[−13] and [−14]
e
[4−1] and [31]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that the matrix [3411] appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for B: B=[3411]⏟P[0002]⏟D[3411]−1⏟P−1

Therefore B is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of B are λ1=0 and λ2=2 and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix P: v1=[31] and v2=[41].

q-37272.name: Question 12
q-37272.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $E$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]E=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
q-37272.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $E:$

$$
E={{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $E$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$

Question 12
?

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix E given that [2131]E=[200−1][2131].

a
[2−3] and [11]
b
[23] and [−11]
c
[−20] and [01]
d
[−13] and [1−2]
e
[20] and [0−1]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that the matrix [2131] appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for E:

E=[2131]−1⏟P[200−1]⏟D[2131]⏟P−1

Therefore, E is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of E are λ1=2 and λ2=−1 and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix P. Computing P, we obtain

P=[2131]−1=1−1[1−1−32]=[−113−2].

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are:

v1=[−13] and v2=[1−2]

q-37605.name: Question 13
q-37605.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
q-37605.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$ 

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]$

q-140133.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $C$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]C=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$
q-140133.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $C:$ 

$$
C={{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $C$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $C$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

q-86693.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
q-86693.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$ 

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]$
